channel.title: Explorations on Open History Map
channel.description: Recent content in Explorations on Open History Map

item.title: Open Culture Map
item.description:
A continent-wide map of cultural heritage: museums, archaeological sites, monuments and artworks pulled from OpenStreetMap and enriched with the identifiers, descriptions and links that Wikidata carries for each one.

Like its sibling editions it refreshes weekly, so the picture keeps pace with the open datasets underneath it. See also Open Wine Map and Open Art Map.

item.title: Open Wine Map
item.description:
A living atlas of wine: every winery and vineyard that OpenStreetMap records, set against the regions and appellations described in Wikidata, so you can see both the individual estates and the named territories they sit inside.

The whole map rebuilds itself weekly, so it tracks the open data as it grows rather than freezing a single snapshot. It is one of the present-day, OSM-plus-Wikidata editions alongside Open Culture Map and Open Art Map.

item.title: Ideas of Ancient Rome
item.description:
Rome is usually told through its rulers and its wars. This edition tells it through its minds: the engineers, jurists, poets and philosophers, and the inventions and ideas they left behind — concrete and aqueducts, law and calendar, rhetoric and road.

Laid out as a single timeline from the traditional founding of the city in 753 BC to the fall of the West in AD 476, and built on Wikidata and Wikipedia. It is the conceptual companion to the Rulers of Ancient Rome gallery.

item.title: Rulers of Ancient Egypt
item.description:
The pharaohs, dynasty by dynasty: from Narmer and the unification of the Two Lands through the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms to Cleopatra VII and the Roman annexation of Egypt.

Built on Wikipedia and Wikidata, it is the direct sibling of Rulers of Ancient Rome — the same portrait-gallery treatment applied to one of the longest continuous lines of rulership in recorded history.

item.title: Rulers of Ancient Rome
item.description:
A portrait gallery of those who held power over Rome across its whole span: the legendary kings, the consuls of the Republic, and the emperors down to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in AD 476.

Each figure is drawn from Wikipedia and Wikidata, with portraits, dates and the line of succession laid out as a single continuous sequence. It is the Roman cut of the broader Rulers of the Past atlas, and a sibling to Rulers of Ancient Egypt.

item.title: Rulers of the Past
item.description:
Most lists of rulers run down a single throne. This one runs across: pick a year and see who was in power everywhere at once — the emperor in Rome, the dynasty in China, the king in a European fragment — laid side by side on one synchronic timeline.

It is assembled from Wikipedia and Wikidata and covers antiquity through the 18th century. The same engine drives the focused sibling editions for Ancient Rome and Ancient Egypt.

item.title: Map of the First World War
item.description:
The Great War rendered day by day: move along the timeline and watch the fronts shift, the battles open and close, and the bombing runs fall, each event placed in space and pinned to its date.

It draws on the THOR bombing dataset, Wikidata for the events and actors, and OpenStreetMap for the underlying geography. It is the elder of the two war atlases — see also Map of the Second World War.

item.title: Map of the Second World War
item.description:
The same day-by-day treatment applied to the Second World War: the war’s reach unfolding across the timeline, with the THOR dataset — the US Department of Defense’s record of aerial bombardment — supplying the operational detail and Wikidata and OpenStreetMap supplying the events and the ground beneath them.

It is the newer of the pair and still settling in; the Map of the First World War is the more finished sibling.

item.title: Open Art Map
item.description:
An atlas built around three places in every artist’s life: where they were born, where they died, and where their work hangs today. Tracing those points turns the history of art into a geography — movements migrating, careers crossing borders, collections gathering far from where they were made.

Assembled from Wikidata for the people and the works and OpenStreetMap for the institutions that hold them, and refreshed monthly. A companion to Open Culture Map.

item.title: Visions of the Past
item.description:
Photography reaches back only to the late 18th century, but people have been making located views of the world for far longer. Visions of the Past gathers those views — photographs, paintings, engravings — and lets you walk among them on a map, choosing both where you stand and when.

It is the public face of the Historical Street View project; the back-end that serves the located views, hsv-api, is listed under Tools.
